title: Search in a Binary Search Tree Problem

content.problemStatement:
You are given the root of a binary search tree (BST) and an integer val. Find the node whose value equals val and return the subtree rooted at that node. If no such node exists, return null.

A BST has values smaller than a node in its left subtree and values greater than a node in its right subtree. The input tree is serialized in level order, with null marking missing children and trailing null values omitted. For this platform, a missing result is serialized as an empty array ([]).

Example 1:
Input: [[4,2,7,1,3],2]
Output: [2,1,3]

Example 2:
Input: [[4,2,7,1,3],5]
Output: []
constraints: root is a valid binary search tree.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array [rootLevelOrder, val], where rootLevelOrder is a level-order array and null denotes a missing child.
content.outputFormat: Single line: JSON-serialized level-order array of the matching subtree, with trailing null values omitted; output [] if the target is absent.

sampleTestCases.explanation: The node with value 2 is found; return its subtree.
No node has value 5, so the serialized result is empty.

notes: The returned subtree is serialized in level order; trailing null values are omitted.
A missing target is serialized as [] to match the sample output convention.

hidden.label: Find a node with two children
Find node with a right child
Subtree with two children and uneven depths

notes: All implementations use BST ordering to avoid scanning unrelated subtrees.

solution.approach: Start at the root. If the current node value equals val, return that node. If val is smaller, move to the left child; otherwise move to the right child. Stop when the value is found or the current node becomes null. Serialize the found subtree in level order, omitting trailing null values; serialize a missing result as [].
solution.timeComplexity: O(h), where h is the height of the BST; O(n) worst case for a skewed tree.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(w) for level-order parsing/serialization queues, where w is the maximum tree width; O(n) worst case.
notes: The search itself uses O(1) auxiliary space iteratively.
The tree serializer omits trailing null entries.

bruteForce.description: Traverse every node until val is found. This ignores the BST ordering and can visit all n nodes.
bruteForce.complexity: Time: O(n); auxiliary search space: O(h) if recursive, O(1) if iterative.

better.description: Use BST ordering to choose the next child at each step, reducing the search path to the height of the tree.
better.complexity: Time: O(h); auxiliary search space: O(1) iteratively.

optimal.description: Iteratively compare val with the current node and move left or right accordingly. Return the matching node or null if the search falls off the tree.
optimal.complexity: Time: O(h); auxiliary search space: O(1), excluding serialization.

hints: Compare val with the current node value before choosing a child.
Use the BST property: smaller values are left, larger values are right.
Return the matching node itself so its entire subtree is preserved.
If the search reaches a null child, the target does not exist.
followUps: What is the worst-case time complexity when the BST is completely skewed?
How would you rebalance the tree to guarantee logarithmic search height?
Can the same search be implemented recursively, and how does its stack space compare?
learningObjectives: Use BST ordering to guide a search.
Return a subtree rooted at a matching node.
Analyze search time in terms of tree height.
